language_wrapper: Consider the sequence {a_n} defined by a_1 = {t}/({t}^2+1) and, for all n ≥ 1, by the relation a_n^2 = a_{n+1} − 2 a_n^2 a_{n+1}. Compute the residue of floor(1/a_{[n]}) modulo {modulus}.
hardness_rationale: The seed reduces via the substitution b_n = 1/a_n to the quadratic map b_{n+1} = b_n^2 − 2 with a specially tuned start b_1 = 5/2, leading to Fermat numbers and a simple power of 2 modulo arithmetic. Our family keeps the same core idea (the same nonlinear recurrence and the key substitution) but parameterizes the initial data as a_1 = t/(t^2+1) so that b_1 = t + 1/t, forcing the general closed form b_n = t^{2^{n−1}} + t^{−2^{n−1}}. Extracting floor(1/a_n) now yields t^{2^{n−1}}, and the modular computation demands nontrivial multiplicative order analysis and exponent reduction modulo lcm of orders modulo distinct prime factors of the composite modulus. The generator enforces that the relevant order has both a substantial 2-adic component and a nontrivial odd component, so simple parity or small-cycle tricks fail. Solvers must recognize the b_{n+1} = b_n^2 − 2 linearization via t + 1/t, then deploy CRT/order reductions, which is a significant step-up in number theoretic sophistication over the seed.
notes: Proof of correctness: Define b_n = 1/a_n. The recurrence a_n^2 = a_{n+1} − 2 a_n^2 a_{n+1} rearranges to a_{n+1} = a_n^2/(1 − 2 a_n^2). Inverting gives b_{n+1} = (1 − 2 a_n^2)/a_n^2 = 1/a_n^2 − 2 = b_n^2 − 2. With a_1 = t/(t^2+1), we have b_1 = (t^2+1)/t = t + 1/t. Inductively, if b_n = t^{2^{n−1}} + t^{−2^{n−1}}, then b_{n+1} = b_n^2 − 2 = (t^{2^{n−1}} + t^{−2^{n−1}})^2 − 2 = t^{2^n} + t^{−2^n}. Hence for all n ≥ 1, b_n = t^{2^{n−1}} + t^{−2^{n−1}}. For t ≥ 2, the fractional term satisfies 0 < t^{−2^{n−1}} < 1, so floor(1/a_n) = floor(b_n) = t^{2^{n−1}}. Therefore the required residue is t^{2^{n−1}} modulo the given modulus. Since gcd(t, modulus)=1, exponent reduction modulo the lcm of the multiplicative orders of t in each prime modulus dividing the composite modulus is valid. The verifier computes ord_lcm, reduces 2^{n−1} modulo ord_lcm without constructing the enormous exponent (via pow(2, n−1, ord_lcm)), and returns pow(t, reduced_exponent, modulus). Difficulty safeguards: The generator ensures ord_lcm has a significant 2-adic valuation and a nontrivial odd part, preventing trivial collapse of the exponent and discouraging simple guessing. This aligns with the intended advanced approach involving algebraic linearization and multiplicative order/CRT techniques.
source_question: Let \(\left\{a_n\right\}\) satisfies \(a_1=\frac{2}{5}, a_n^2=a_{n+1}-2 a_n^2 a_{n+1}\), find the residue of \(\left[\frac{1}{a_{2025}}\right]\) mod 407.
